Chapter 22
SDN Controllers

This manual replaces Chapter 22 of CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (Exam 200-301) by Todd Lammle (2020), book pages 689 to 742. It follows the book's order. It adds simple explanations, command breakdowns, labs and quizzes, and it marks every place where this document differs from the book.

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Learning objectives. The book lists these exam topics for this chapter (v1.0 wording): 1.1.e Controllers (Cisco DNA Center and WLC); 6.2 Compare traditional networks with controller-based networking; 6.3 Describe controller-based and software defined architectures (overlay, underlay, and fabric), with 6.3.a Separation of control plane and data plane and 6.3.b North-bound and south-bound APIs; 6.4 Compare traditional campus device management with Cisco DNA Center enabled device management.
After this chapter you should be able to:
1. Explain what an NMS and an NCM do, and how SNMP, traps and syslog fit in.
2. Name the management, control and data planes and say what runs in each.
3. Explain what SDN is, and what the northbound and southbound interfaces are.
4. Compare the campus (3-tier) and spine/leaf (Clos) architectures.
5. Explain underlay, overlay and fabric.
6. Describe what a controller such as Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center) adds compared with traditional tools and with manual work.
VERIFY

BOOK Book pages 690 and 691. A network team learns about problems in two ways: angry users, or a Network Monitoring System (NMS) that alerts them. An NMS continuously polls your devices using SNMP so it can spot misbehaving ones. It also records performance such as ICMP response times, how much traffic flows, and (depending on the product) applications and VoIP call quality.
- By default an NMS polls devices about every couple of minutes.
- A device can also send an SNMP trap on its own, for example when an interface goes down.
- Alerts can go out as email, SMS (for the person on call), or as an alert on a screen in the Network Operations Center.
The book demonstrates SolarWinds Network Performance Monitor and mentions Cisco Prime Infrastructure.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says DNA Center is the successor of Prime Infrastructure. Cisco's product page says Prime Infrastructure 3.10 is no longer sold (end of sale 29 September 2023, end of support 30 September 2028) and tells users to consider switching to Cisco Catalyst Center or Cisco Meraki Dashboard. Cisco's data sheet says Catalyst Center is the former Cisco DNA Center. Verification: official Cisco pages.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED SNMP in plain words. An SNMP manager (the NMS) asks an SNMP agent (on the device) for values, or the agent sends an unrequested trap or inform. The values live in a MIB and each has an OID (a number path). Versions: SNMPv1 and v2c use a plain-text community string (like a password); SNMPv3 adds real authentication and encryption. Polls and requests normally use UDP 161, and traps use UDP 162. CHECK (general knowledge)
22.1.1 Configuring SNMP
BOOK Book pages 691 and 692. The book configures a Catalyst 3750X switch.
SNMP and traps BOOK
C3750X-SW01(config)#snmp-server community testlabRO RO
C3750X-SW01(config)#snmp-server community testlabRW RW
C3750X-SW01(config)#snmp-server host 10.20.2.115 traps testlabTRAPS
C3750X-SW01(config)#snmp-server source-interface traps vlan 310
C3750X-SW01(config)#snmp-server enable traps
- snmp-server community testlabRO RO creates a read-only community string. The NMS can read but not change.
- snmp-server community testlabRW RW creates a read-write community string. The NMS can also make changes. This is more dangerous.
- snmp-server host 10.20.2.115 traps testlabTRAPS tells the switch where to send traps, and which community string to use for them.
- snmp-server source-interface traps vlan 310 chooses which interface's address the traps come from.
- snmp-server enable traps turns on all supported traps. Add one trap name to enable just that one, and use no to turn one off. Type snmp-server enable traps ? to see the list on your device.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED Use SNMPv3 where you can. The book uses community strings (SNMPv1/v2c), which travel in plain text, and a read-write string with an easy name. In real networks: use SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption, limit which hosts may use a community with an ACL (this ties back to Chapter 10: snmp-server community <string> RO <acl>), and avoid read-write unless needed. CHECK for the exact commands on your IOS version.
SNMPv3 example ADDED CHECK (syntax varies by version)
snmp-server group NMS-GROUP v3 priv
snmp-server user NMS-USER NMS-GROUP v3 auth sha <auth-password> priv aes 128 <priv-password>
snmp-server host 10.20.2.115 traps version 3 priv NMS-USER
22.1.2 Network Health
BOOK Book pages 692 and 693. An NMS usually shows device status with three colours:
| Colour | Meaning |
| Green | Healthy nodes with no reported problems. |
| Yellow | Nodes that are up, but have reported issues, such as an interface that is down or a failed fan. |
| Red | Nodes that are not reachable and are probably down. |

The NMS has default rules about how to treat events (an interface down, a router reboot). Every NMS lets you customise alerts. The book jokes that with an open source NMS you may end up writing Java code at 3 a.m.
22.1.3 Central Syslog

BOOK Book pages 694 and 695. An NMS can also be the central syslog server. You can search and filter the many messages, and create rules, for example to run a script when an OSPF-related message arrives.
Send syslog to the NMS BOOK
CSR31(config)#logging trap debugging
CSR31(config)#logging host 10.20.2.115
- logging trap debugging sets the severity level of messages sent to the syslog server. debugging is level 7, the highest and noisiest.
- logging host 10.20.2.115 sets the IP address of the syslog server.
| Level | Name | Meaning |
| 0 | emergencies | System unusable |
| 1 | alerts | Immediate action needed |
| 2 | critical | Critical condition |
| 3 | errors | Error condition |
| 4 | warnings | Warning condition |
| 5 | notifications | Normal but significant condition |
| 6 | informational | Informational message |
| 7 | debugging | Debugging messages |
MEMORY TIP
Lower number = more severe. A setting of level N sends level N and all lower numbers. So logging trap warnings (4) sends levels 0 to 4.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Why the book's level 7 is only for demos. debugging sends everything and floods the server. Real networks usually use informational (6) or notifications (5). The v2.0 exam (objective 5.6) asks you to interpret syslog messages, severity levels and facilities. A Cisco message looks like %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down: a facility (LINK), a severity number (3) and a mnemonic (UPDOWN). The level numbers above were checked against the standard list. CHECK for the exact message wording and for the "facility" meaning, because syslog itself also uses facility codes such as local0 to local7.
22.1.4 Central SNMP Traps

BOOK Book page 695. Traps show up on the NMS much like syslog messages. The main difference: traps usually give a lot more detail than log messages. You can search by keyword, filter by device and set rules, for example to run something when a trap arrives.
22.1.5 Interface Information

BOOK Book pages 695 to 697. The NMS can graph interface utilization (how busy), a buffer misses graph (buffers overloaded) and an interface error graph. It can also show the interface description and the assigned VLAN name.
22.1.6 Hardware Health

BOOK Book page 697. Hardware health is hard to follow manually unless you are on the box or notice a log message. The NMS presents an easy graph, so a failing part is noticed before "the router blows up at 2 a.m.".
22.1.7 Network Information

BOOK Book pages 697 to 699. Two graphs the book highlights: Response Time and Packet Loss (good for "slow Internet" calls) and CPU Load and Memory Utilization (is the router healthy, should it be upgraded). The NMS also uses CDP information to see which devices are attached and which VLANs exist. It reads routing tables to detect route flapping (a route appearing and disappearing repeatedly) and can show whether a switch is in a stack.
VERIFY
CHECK All screenshots (Figures 22.1 to 22.9) are from a 2019 SolarWinds lab. Product names, screens and features have changed since. Learn the ideas, not the screens.
Quick check 22.1
Q1. Which protocol does an NMS use to poll devices?
A. Telnet
B. SNMP
C. SMTP
D. RESTCONF
Answer: B - the book says an NMS polls devices using SNMP.
Q2. What is the difference between an SNMP poll and an SNMP trap?
Answer: A poll is requested by the NMS. A trap is sent by the device on its own when something happens - traps usually carry more detail than syslog messages.
Q3. Which syslog level number is "debugging", and is it more or less severe than "errors"?
Answer: Level 7, and it is the least severe - lower numbers are more severe. Errors is level 3.
Q4. Which command sets the IP address of the syslog server?
A. logging trap 10.20.2.115
B. logging host 10.20.2.115
C. snmp-server host 10.20.2.115
D. syslog server 10.20.2.115
Answer: B - logging host sets the server. logging trap sets the severity level.
Q5. Why is a read-write SNMP community string risky?
Answer: A device that knows it can change the configuration, and community strings travel in plain text - use SNMPv3 and ACLs where possible. ADDED

BOOK Book pages 699 to 702. Monitoring tells you something is wrong. A Network Configuration Manager (NCM) manages your configurations. The book's question: if your main Internet router fails, do you copy and paste an old config from Notepad? A busy router can have hundreds or thousands of lines.
An NCM can be the same server as the NMS, or a separate one. What it does:
- Backs up configurations by connecting to each device and copying the config to the server. Devices can also tell the NCM when a change happens.
- Lets you search saved configs for keywords.
- Lets you compare two versions to see what changed (useful after a crash or before a disaster).
- Lets you push configurations, and use templates with its own scripting language to make mass changes. Every NCM uses a different scripting engine.
Let the NCM log in to a router BOOK
CSR31(config)#aaa new-model
CSR31(config)#aaa authentication login default local
CSR31(config)#username ncm secret ncmPass
CSR31(config)#enable sec ncmEnable
- aaa new-model turns on the AAA system.
- aaa authentication login default local makes logins check the local user list.
- username ncm secret ncmPass creates a user for the NCM. The secret keyword stores the password hashed.
- enable sec ncmEnable is the short form of enable secret ncmEnable. It sets the privileged mode password.
The NCM must be able to Telnet or SSH into the device. NCMs can also use the SNMP read-write community to make changes.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED Use SSH, not Telnet, for NCM access, and never copy the book's example passwords (ncmPass, ncmEnable): they are lab values. SSH needs a hostname, a domain name and RSA keys on the device (the book's DNA Center upgrade pre-checks mention the same requirements). The book's answer key for Chapter 22, question 15, lists Telnet as an NCM protocol. Treat Telnet as a legacy answer.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

BOOK The book says DNA Center uses Apache Velocity for templates (section 22.8.3). SolarWinds has a similar template feature with its own language (Figure 22.12). Figures 22.10 to 22.12 show the config overview, compare and push screens.
NMS, NCM and manual work
| Task | Manual | NMS | NCM |
| Know which devices are healthy | Log in to each device | Dashboard from SNMP polling | Not its job |
| Hear about a failure | Users complain | Traps, syslog, alerts | Not its job |
| Back up configs | Copy and paste into Notepad | Not its job | Scheduled backups |
| See what changed | Compare by eye | Not its job | Compare saved versions |
| Make a change on many devices | Log in to each one | Not its job | Push config, templates |
MEMORY TIP
Short version: NMS = watch and alert (SNMP, syslog). NCM = back up, compare and push configs (SSH or Telnet, SNMP read-write). A controller such as Catalyst Center does both and more.
Quick check 22.2
Q1. Name three things an NCM does.
Answer: Any three of: back up configs, search configs, compare versions, push configs, templates - these are the main NCM functions in the book.
Q2. What does the secret keyword do in username ncm secret ncmPass?
Answer: Stores the password in a hashed form - it is safer than a plain password entry.
Q3. Which is better for NCM login, Telnet or SSH, and why?
Answer: SSH, because Telnet sends everything in plain text - this is an update to the book's answer key. UPDATED
Q4. Which tool would you use to see what changed in a router's config last night?
A. NMS
B. NCM
C. A syslog filter
D. A ping
Answer: B - an NCM can compare saved configuration versions.

BOOK Book pages 702 to 706. To understand SDN you first need to see how a normal router sends a packet. Before it can forward, a router needs routes, learned from a static route, a default route or a routing protocol. The book uses OSPF for the example (the CCNA focuses on OSPF). The router then looks up the destination (Cisco uses Cisco Express Forwarding, CEF), needs an ARP entry for the next hop, decreases the TTL by one, and recalculates the IP header and Ethernet frame checksums before sending.
Routers split these jobs into three planes:
| Plane | Job | Examples in the book |
| Management plane | Everything about logging in to and managing the device | Telnet, SSH, SNMP, HTTP and HTTPS (web interface), APIs such as REST, console port, AUX port, management port |

| Control plane | The brain. Runs the protocols and makes the decisions, to build the forwarding information | Routing protocols such as OSPF (adjacencies, route learning), ARP, STP, VTP, MAC address tables, QoS, CDP and LLDP, and the defining of ACLs and NAT |

| Data plane | The workhorse. Uses what the control plane built to forward the traffic | Encapsulating and de-encapsulating, adding and removing headers, dropping traffic that hits an ACL deny, moving the packet from the inbound to the outbound interface |
EXAM CRITICAL

Plane quick sort. Management = how you reach the box (SSH, SNMP, HTTPS, console). Control = protocols and decisions (OSPF, ARP, STP, CDP/LLDP). Data = forwarding the actual traffic (the data plane does not run protocols).
VERIFY

CHECK The book (page 703, and question 6 and its answer) puts CDP and LLDP in the control plane. Other sources put neighbour-discovery protocols elsewhere. For this exam, follow the book's classification. Also note the book says ACLs and NAT are defined in the control plane but drops traffic in the data plane: think of it as you define the rule, the data plane enforces it.
22.3.1 Management Plane

BOOK Book pages 702 and 703. Covers logging in (Telnet, SSH, not that we would ever use Telnet), SNMP (so an NMS can poll), HTTP and HTTPS, APIs (including REST, from the Automation chapter), and the console, AUX and management ports. In modern IOS-XE the web interface is much nicer than in early IOS (Figure 22.13).
22.3.2 Control Plane
BOOK Book page 703. The brain of the router: all the protocols run here and all the decisions are made. The goal is to produce the information needed to send the packet towards its destination.
22.3.3 Data Plane
BOOK Book pages 703 and 704. Everything that happens here directly affects traffic. It uses the control plane information to forward the packet.
22.3.4 Forwarding
BOOK Book pages 704 to 706. The book follows R02 forwarding a packet from R01 to R03 (Figures 22.14 and 22.15):
- OSPF on R02 forms adjacencies with R01 and R03, and the control plane receives routes in LSAs.
- The LSAs go into the Link State Database (LSDB). It contains type 1 LSAs for each router and type 2 LSAs for DRs (unless the OSPF network type is changed).
- Neighbour information is kept in the neighbour table.
- The neighbour table and the LSDB feed the routing table, where the best route is chosen (lowest metric, lowest administrative distance, longest match).
Then, on the data plane side:
- CEF takes the best routes from the routing table and installs them in the Forwarding Information Base (FIB).
- The ARP table is used to build the adjacency table. The forwarding table needs ARP resolved for the next hop before the route is valid.
- The information is pushed to hardware for forwarding.
How the tables relate (same idea as Figures 22.14 and 22.15) BOOK CHECK
Control plane: Static routes / OSPF -> Neighbor table + LSDB -> Routing table ARP table
Data plane: Incoming interface -> Forwarding table (FIB) + Adjacency table -> Outgoing interface
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Commands to look at these tables on a Cisco router: show ip route (routing table), show ip ospf neighbor, show ip cef (FIB), show adjacency (adjacency table), show ip arp. The book says the full CEF story is outside the CCNA. CHECK for exact output on your platform.
The book finishes with a reason SDN matters: adding a new VM in a traditional 3-tier network. The steps for a new VLAN and subnet that needs Internet access (Figure 22.16):
| # | Task in a traditional network |
| 1 | Choose a new VLAN and subnet (hopefully with an IP address management tool). |
| 2 | Make sure the VLAN exists on all switches (VTP can help). |
| 3 | Configure STP so the new VLAN has the right root switch. |
| 4 | Add the VLAN to trunk allow lists. |
| 5 | Create an SVI on each distribution switch, and use an FHRP. |
| 6 | Add the new subnet to the routing protocol. |
| 7 | Update firewall rules, and configure NAT. |
| 8 | Adjust external routing, depending on requirements. |
Doing this often is slow and risky: it needs planning, change control, and clean-up when the VM is gone. This is the pain that a controller can automate.
Quick check 22.3
Q1. Which plane does SSH belong to?
A. Management
B. Control
C. Data
D. None of them
Answer: A - SSH, Telnet, SNMP and HTTPS are management plane.
Q2. Which plane runs OSPF?
Answer: The control plane - the control plane runs protocols and makes decisions.
Q3. Which plane drops a packet that hits an ACL deny?
Answer: The data plane - the data plane enforces the rule on actual traffic.
Q4. What does CEF build from the routing table?
Answer: The Forwarding Information Base (FIB) - the adjacency table is built from ARP.
Q5. What does the data plane do about protocols?
Answer: It does not run protocols; it forwards traffic - the book's answer to review question 7.

BOOK Book pages 706 to 709. An SDN solution has two important interfaces. You reach the controller through the Northbound Interface (NBI), which is similar to the management plane. The controller reaches the network devices through the Southbound Interface (SBI).
SDN architecture (same idea as Figure 22.17) BOOK
Users / Scripts
API
Northbound Interface (NBI)
SDN Controller (control plane)
Southbound Interface (SBI)
Network devices (data plane)
22.4.1 Northbound Interfaces

BOOK Book page 707. You use the NBI to get something done through the controller, usually with a GUI (for example in Meraki) or a RESTful API call inside a script. You can use any scripting language, because all the script does is call the REST API. Through the NBI you can create VLANs, list devices, poll network health, and even automate the VM scenario above.
EXAM CRITICAL
NBI = how users, scripts and apps talk to the controller (REST API, GUI). SBI = how the controller talks to the devices.
22.4.2 Southbound Interfaces
BOOK Book page 708. There are many ways for the controller to talk to devices. The book lists four:
| SBI | What the book says | Today |

| OpenFlow | Industry-standard API defined by the ONF. Configures non-proprietary "white label" switches and determines the flow path. Sends detailed, complex instructions to the control plane of the elements: an imperative SDN model. Used by OpenDaylight. | Cisco prefers its own solutions because of OpenFlow limits (book). |
| NETCONF | IETF-standard network management protocol. With RPC you install, change and delete device configuration, using XML. | Widely used. See the verified facts below. |
| onePK | Cisco-proprietary. Lets you inspect or change device configuration. SDKs for Java, C and Python. | Legacy, though still found (book). |

| OpFlex | Used by Cisco ACI. A declarative model: the controller (Cisco calls it the APIC) sends a more abstract "summary policy", and the devices apply it with their own (partly centralised) control planes. | Used by ACI. |
|  | Imperative | Declarative |
| What the controller sends | Detailed, step-by-step instructions | The desired result (a summary policy) |
| Who works out the details | The controller | The devices, with their own control planes |
| Example in the book | OpenFlow | OpFlex (Cisco ACI) |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED NETCONF facts, checked against Cisco IOS XE documents: NETCONF is defined in RFC 6241, uses XML and an RPC mechanism, runs over SSH with TCP port 830 as the default, and models data with YANG. RESTCONF (RFC 8040) is the related YANG-based, REST-like interface. The book does not mention YANG or RESTCONF. ADDED
VERIFY

CHECK The book says of OpenFlow: "All configuration is done via NETCONF." OpenFlow itself programs flow entries in a switch. Configuring the switch (ports, controller address) through NETCONF is a separate ONF specification called OF-Config. Treat the book's sentence as too simple. The review answer you need is: OpenDaylight uses OpenFlow.
22.4.3 SDN Solutions
BOOK Book pages 708 and 709. Controllers you may meet:
| Solution | Book says | Note |
| Cisco APIC-EM | Cisco's first enterprise SDN controller, focused on IWAN. Legacy. Succeeded by DNA Center. | Legacy. BOOK |
| Cisco DNA Center | Cisco's main enterprise SDN controller. | Now called Cisco Catalyst Center (Cisco data sheet). UPDATED |
| Cisco ACI | Cisco's data center SDN solution (APIC controller). | Data Center track. |
| Cisco SD-WAN | Brings SDN to the WAN. | Cisco has renamed parts of this product line. CHECK |
| OpenDaylight (ODL) | Popular open source OpenFlow controller (Figure 22.18). | Cisco gives limited OpenFlow support. |
Quick check 22.4
Q1. What is the northbound interface used for?
A. Talking to the network devices
B. Letting users and scripts interact with the controller
C. Tracking AP performance
D. Routing traffic out of the network
Answer: B - the NBI is how you reach the controller, usually through a GUI or REST API.
Q2. Which southbound protocol does OpenDaylight use, and which does Cisco ACI use?
Answer: OpenFlow for OpenDaylight and OpFlex for ACI - the book's review questions 8 and 9.
Q3. Which model sends detailed instructions: imperative or declarative?
Answer: Imperative (OpenFlow) - OpFlex is declarative and sends a summary policy.
Q4. NETCONF uses which transport and default port?
Answer: SSH and TCP port 830 - Cisco IOS XE documentation. ADDED
Q5. Which Cisco SBI is legacy?
Answer: onePK - the book says it is legacy but may still be found.

BOOK Book pages 709 and 710. "SDN" can mean many things, but it generally means separating the control plane from the data plane on a network device. Devices can then be managed centrally by a controller instead of one at a time.
Separating the control plane (same idea as Figures 22.19 and 22.20) BOOK
Traditional: Controller-based (SDN):
[Control plane] [Control plane] [ SDN Controller: control plane ]
[Data plane]--trunk--[Data plane] [Data plane]--trunk--[Data plane]
Each device has its own control plane. One central control plane; devices only forward.

Meraki is the book's example. Everything in the Meraki line is managed from the cloud, so the devices mostly provide the data plane. Good: you can manage everything from anywhere (there is even an app). Bad: devices must reach the Meraki cloud before you can manage them, which is awkward when you are trying to fix an outage. Meraki does give basic local management tools to help troubleshoot connection problems (Figure 22.20).
VERIFY

CHECK The book says Meraki devices "really only provide the data plane". That is a simplification. The cloud is for management. Devices still forward traffic when the cloud cannot be reached, though you lose central management. The exam point is the idea of a cloud-managed, controller-based model (v2.0 objective 5.3 lists cloud-based and controller-based approaches).
Quick check 22.5
Q1. What does SDN generally mean?
Answer: Separating the control plane from the data plane - the controller holds the intelligence.
Q2. Name one advantage and one disadvantage of the cloud-managed Meraki model.
Answer: Advantage: manage from anywhere. Disadvantage: devices must reach the cloud before you can manage them - the book's two points.

BOOK Book pages 710 and 711. A good example is the Cisco Wireless LAN Controller (WLC). The access points that join the WLC are not clever alone, so they rely on the controller to push their configuration. DNA Center goes further and lets you manage network device configuration centrally through applications that run on the controller.
| Advantage | Disadvantage |

| Change a setting once and it is copied to all relevant devices. Configuration is consistent everywhere and typing mistakes on 50 switches are avoided. | A mistake in a template is pushed everywhere at once. The book's example: typing switchport trunk allowed vlan 10 instead of switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10 on one switch is an outage you can fix. Pushing that to all switches is a disaster. |

22.6.1 Campus Architecture
BOOK Book page 711. The campus architecture is the traditional hierarchy. It is easy to troubleshoot because each layer has a clear job (like the OSI model).
| Layer | Job |

| Access | Endpoints connect here. VLANs are assigned. Port-level features such as port security and 802.1X are applied. Usually only Layer 2 (no Layer 3 except management), so cheaper switches work. |
| Distribution | Hosts the SVIs and IP services such as DHCP relay. Layer 2 links down to access switches, Layer 3 links up to core. Runs a routing protocol with the core. |
| Core | High-speed routing between distribution switches. No other services. |
22.6.2 Spine/Leaf Architecture
BOOK Book page 712. The spine/leaf design (also called Clos) is the new, preferred architecture for controller-based networks and data centers. It has two kinds of switch:
| Switch | Role |
| Leaf | Where devices connect. Maps to the access and distribution layers of the 3-tier model. Each leaf has a high-bandwidth uplink to each spine. |
| Spine | Like the core: its only job is fast transport between the leaf switches. |
- Leaf switches connect only to spine switches, never to other leaf switches. Every destination in the fabric follows the same path: Leaf to Spine to Leaf.
- Because the paths are the same length, traffic is easily load balanced with equal-cost multipath (ECMP).
- Easy to grow: need more ports? Add a leaf. Need more bandwidth? Add a spine.
| Design | Devices | Links (script-checked) | Path between two edge devices |
| Full mesh of 8 switches | 8 | 28 | Direct, but links grow very fast (16 switches need 120 links) |
| Spine/leaf with 2 spines and 8 leaves | 10 | 16 | Leaf to spine to leaf, with 2 equal-cost paths |
| Spine/leaf with 4 spines and 16 leaves | 20 | 64 | Leaf to spine to leaf, with 4 equal-cost paths |

22.7.1 Underlay

BOOK Book pages 713 to 716. The underlay is the physical network that gives connectivity so the overlay can be built on it. It has basic configuration, and its job is mostly to advertise each device's loopback IP into OSPF (or IS-IS, which is beyond the CCNA). Devices are cabled for high redundancy. A full mesh gives maximum redundancy but gets out of hand as the network grows.
The book builds the underlay in four parts: MTU, interface configuration, OSPF configuration and verification.
MTU
The underlay carries larger packets than a normal network, so the book raises the MTU on the underlay switches.
Raise MTU, enable routing BOOK (shortened)
SW01(config)#system mtu ?
<1500-9198> MTU size in bytes
SW01(config)#system mtu 9000
Global Ethernet MTU is set to 9000 bytes.
SW01(config)#do reload
SW01(config)#ip routing
- system mtu 9000 sets the Ethernet payload size. On this platform the switch must be reloaded.
- ip routing turns the switch into a Layer 3 switch so it can run a routing protocol.
EXAM CRITICAL

OSPF needs matching MTUs on both ends of a neighbour relationship. If you change the MTU on one switch, change it on its neighbours too, or add ip ospf mtu-ignore on the neighbouring interfaces to get around it without changing the MTU.

Interface configuration

BOOK It is a bad idea to use STP in the underlay: STP blocks redundant links, which wastes fast uplinks (10, 40, 100 Gb/s). The better way: use only Layer 3 interfaces. Then STP does not run, nothing is blocked, loops are not a problem (routing handles it), and the routing table can load balance across links with ECMP.
Layer 3 underlay interfaces BOOK (shortened)

SW01(config-if)#no switchport
SW01(config-if)#ip address 10.1.21.1 255.255.255.0
SW01(config-if)#ip ospf network point-to-point
(repeated for g3/1, g3/2, g3/3, g2/2, g2/3 with their own addresses)
SW01(config-if)#interface loopback 0
- no switchport turns the port into a routed (Layer 3) port.
- ip address ... gives it an IP address.
- ip ospf network point-to-point sets the OSPF network type to point-to-point, so there is no DR/BDR election.
- interface loopback 0 and a /32 address give each switch a stable identity for the overlay later.

| Overlay | Virtual network tunnelled over the underlay (VXLAN). Services such as security and QoS live here. DMVPN is a WAN overlay. |
| Fabric | All the devices that use the SDN solution (underlay plus overlay). |

| Catalyst Center | Formerly DNA Center. Discovery, Hierarchy, Templates, Topology, Upgrades, Command Runner (show only), Assurance, Path Trace, EasyQoS, LAN Automation (PnP), SD-Access (LISP, VXLAN, TrustSec), REST API. |
| v2.0 objective | 5.3 Describe network management approaches (device-based, cloud-based, controller-based, automation-based, infrastructure as code). Also 5.4 SNMP and 5.6 syslog. |

content.text: VERIFY
Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware, on a Cisco simulator or in Packet Tracer. All commands and outputs are examples that may differ on your platform or software version.

ADDED Labs 1 and 2 use Cisco Packet Tracer. Lab 3 uses Cisco's free DevNet sandbox, so it needs no equipment but depends on that sandbox being available. Interface names, supported commands and outputs differ between Packet Tracer versions and from real devices, so every expected result is tagged CHECK . Record what you actually saw in the Self-Assessment table and in your Notion tracker. Do not mark anything as Know until you can repeat it unaided.

Build 2 spine and 3 leaf multilayer switches (for example 3650 or 3560 models in Packet Tracer). Every leaf connects to every spine, and leaves do not connect to each other. This gives 6 links. The addresses were checked by script: no overlaps, and the loopbacks sit outside the link pool.
| Link | Spine side | Leaf side |
| Device | Loopback 0 |
VERIFY

CHECK Packet Tracer switches may not accept a /31 mask on a routed port. If yours does not, use /30 links instead (for example 10.255.0.0/30 for each link, using the .1 and .2 addresses) and keep the rest of the lab the same.
1. Cable the 6 links. Use any free ports, and write down which port goes where.
On SPINE1 (repeat the same pattern with its own addresses on SPINE2; on each leaf use its own link and loopback addresses from the tables):
Lab 1: SPINE1 (port names vary)
SPINE1(config)#ip routing
SPINE1(config)#interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
SPINE1(config-if)#no switchport
SPINE1(config-if)#ip address 10.255.0.0 255.255.255.254
SPINE1(config-if)#ip ospf network point-to-point
SPINE1(config-if)#no shutdown
(repeat for the links to LEAF2 and LEAF3 with 10.255.0.2 and 10.255.0.4)
SPINE1(config)#interface loopback 0
SPINE1(config-if)#ip address 10.255.255.1 255.255.255.255
SPINE1(config)#router ospf 1
SPINE1(config-router)#network 10.255.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0
- ip routing makes the switch route.
- no switchport makes the port a routed port. There is no STP on it.
- ip ospf network point-to-point removes the DR/BDR election.
- The network 10.255.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0 line covers both the links (10.255.0.x) and the loopbacks (10.255.255.x). This uses a normal wildcard instead of the book's all-zeros shortcut.
2. Configure LEAF1, LEAF2 and LEAF3 in the same way: two routed ports (one to each spine), a loopback, and the same OSPF command.
3. Verify neighbours. On LEAF1 run show ip ospf neighbor. Expected: two neighbours (SPINE1 and SPINE2), state FULL with no DR/BDR (shown as -). CHECK
4. Verify ECMP. On LEAF1 run show ip route ospf. Expected: the loopback of LEAF2 (10.255.255.12) has two equal-cost next hops, one through each spine. CHECK

5. Prove the path. Ping 10.255.255.12 from LEAF1, using its own loopback as the source: ping 10.255.255.12 source loopback 0. Then run traceroute 10.255.255.12 source loopback 0. Expected: it succeeds and crosses exactly one spine (leaf, spine, leaf). CHECK
6. Break and fix. Shut one uplink on LEAF1 (shutdown). Run show ip route ospf again. Expected: only one path remains. Re-enable the port. Expected: two paths return after OSPF converges. CHECK
7. Scale it. Add LEAF4 (new loopback 10.255.255.14/32, new /31 links 10.255.0.12 and 10.255.0.14). Notice that you did not have to touch the existing leaves. That is the spine/leaf growth rule.
WHY THIS MATTERS
This lab shows the book's underlay ideas: Layer 3 only, no STP, OSPF on loopbacks, ECMP, and simple scaling.
Topology: one router (R1), one switch, and a Server-PT (Packet Tracer server) at 10.255.100.10/24 on the same LAN as R1's interface 10.255.100.1/24 (both addresses checked by script).
1. Configure R1's LAN interface 10.255.100.1/24 and the server address 10.255.100.10/24 with gateway 10.255.100.1. Ping from R1 to the server. Expected: success.
Lab 2 configuration (SNMP commands may be limited in Packet Tracer) CHECK
R1(config)#logging host 10.255.100.10
R1(config)#logging trap informational
R1(config)#access-list 10 permit host 10.255.100.10
R1(config)#snmp-server community labRO RO 10
R1(config)#snmp-server host 10.255.100.10 traps labTRAPS
R1(config)#snmp-server enable traps
- logging host sends syslog to the server. logging trap informational sends levels 0 to 6.
- access-list 10 permit host 10.255.100.10 plus the 10 at the end of the community command restricts that community to the NMS address (a Chapter 10 idea).
- The SNMP lines are the book's commands, with an ACL added.
2. On the server open Services, then SYSLOG, and turn it on.

3. On R1 make an event: interface GigabitEthernet0/0, shutdown, then no shutdown. Expected: messages like %LINK-5-CHANGED and %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN appear on the router, and (if the server's syslog service works in your version) on the server. CHECK
4. Run show logging on R1 and note the severity number in each message. Practise reading the facility, severity and mnemonic.
5. Change to logging trap errors and repeat step 3. Expected: the level 5 messages no longer reach the server, because 5 is less severe than 3. CHECK
6. Run show snmp and show running-config | include snmp. Record what you see. CHECK Packet Tracer may not include a working SNMP manager; the aim is to practise the commands.

labs.title: Lab 3 (optional): Call a controller's REST API

content.text: This lab needs no equipment. It uses the Cisco DevNet Catalyst Center Always-On sandbox, which Cisco documents as a free, 24x7 hosted lab. Community posts show that it sometimes goes down and that the Always-On devices only accept read (GET) requests. CHECK Take the address and the published read-only credentials from Cisco's own sandbox page, and do not save them in your notes.
1. Open Cisco's Catalyst Center sandbox page on developer.cisco.com and read the Always-On sandbox instructions.
2. Use Postman or curl to request an authentication token from the sandbox (a POST to its auth path). Cisco's Getting Started page gives the path and the headers. CHECK
3. Use the token in a header to GET the list of network devices through the Intent API. CHECK
4. Read the JSON you get back. Write down three fields you see for the first device (for example its type and its management IP address).

5. Connect the dots: you just used the northbound interface of a controller. The controller then uses its southbound protocols (SSH, SNMP, NETCONF) to talk to the devices. You never logged in to a device.

content.text: Q1 Which protocol does an NMS use to poll devices?
A. Telnet
B. SNMP
C. SMTP
D. RESTCONF
Answer: B - the book says an NMS polls devices using SNMP.
Q2 What is the difference between an SNMP poll and an SNMP trap?
Answer: A - poll is requested by the NMS. A trap is sent by the device on its own when something happens - traps usually carry more detail than syslog messages.
Q3 Which syslog level number is "debugging", and is it more or less severe than "errors"?
Answer: Level 7, and it is the least severe - lower numbers are more severe. Errors is level 3.
Q4 Which command sets the IP address of the syslog server?
A. logging trap 10.20.2.115
B. logging host 10.20.2.115
C. snmp-server host 10.20.2.115
D. syslog server 10.20.2.115
Answer: B - logging host sets the server. logging trap sets the severity level.
Q5 Why is a read-write SNMP community string risky?
Answer: A - device that knows it can change the configuration, and community strings travel in plain text - use SNMPv3 and ACLs where possible. ADDED
Q1 Name three things an NCM does.
Answer: A - ny three of: back up configs, search configs, compare versions, push configs, templates - these are the main NCM functions in the book.
Q2 What does the secret keyword do in username ncm secret ncmPass?
Answer: Stores the password in a hashed form - it is safer than a plain password entry.
Q3 Which is better for NCM login, Telnet or SSH, and why?
Answer: SSH, because Telnet sends everything in plain text - this is an update to the book's answer key. UPDATED
Q4 Which tool would you use to see what changed in a router's config last night?
A. NMS
B. NCM
C. A syslog filter
D. A ping
Answer: B - an NCM can compare saved configuration versions.
Q1 Which plane does SSH belong to?
A. Management
B. Control
C. Data
D. None of them
Answer: A - SSH, Telnet, SNMP and HTTPS are management plane.
Q2 Which plane runs OSPF?
Answer: The control plane - the control plane runs protocols and makes decisions.
Q3 Which plane drops a packet that hits an ACL deny?
Answer: The data plane - the data plane enforces the rule on actual traffic.
Q4 What does CEF build from the routing table?
Answer: The Forwarding Information Base (FIB) - the adjacency table is built from ARP.
Q5 What does the data plane do about protocols?
Answer: It does not run protocols; it forwards traffic - the book's answer to review question 7.
Q1 What is the northbound interface used for?
A. Talking to the network devices
B. Letting users and scripts interact with the controller
C. Tracking AP performance
D. Routing traffic out of the network
Answer: B - the NBI is how you reach the controller, usually through a GUI or REST API.
Q2 Which southbound protocol does OpenDaylight use, and which does Cisco ACI use?
Answer: OpenFlow for OpenDaylight and OpFlex for ACI - the book's review questions 8 and 9.
Q3 Which model sends detailed instructions: imperative or declarative?
Answer: Imperative (OpenFlow) - OpFlex is declarative and sends a summary policy.
Q4 NETCONF uses which transport and default port?
Answer: SSH and TCP port 830 - Cisco IOS XE documentation. ADDED
Q5 Which Cisco SBI is legacy?
Answer: onePK - the book says it is legacy but may still be found.
Q1 What does SDN generally mean?
Answer: Separating the control plane from the data plane - the controller holds the intelligence.
Q2 Name one advantage and one disadvantage of the cloud-managed Meraki model.
Answer: A - dvantage: manage from anywhere. Disadvantage: devices must reach the cloud before you can manage them - the book's two points.
Q1 Name two advantages of controller-based networking.
Answer: A - ny two of: central management, mass configuration, consistent configuration, central monitoring and scripting - the book lists these.
Q2 Which layer of the campus architecture hosts the SVIs?
A. Access
B. Distribution
C. Core
D. Spine
Answer: B - the distribution layer hosts SVIs, DHCP relay and the Layer 3 boundary.
Q3 In spine/leaf, which devices does a leaf switch connect to?
Answer: Only spine switches - leaf switches do not connect to other leaf switches.
Q4 How do you add more ports, and how do you add more bandwidth, in spine/leaf?
Answer: A - dd a leaf for ports. Add a spine for bandwidth - the book's growth rule.
Q5 What load-balancing method does spine/leaf make easy?
Answer: ECMP (equal-cost multipath) - paths are equal length.
Q1 What is the underlay?
A. A layer where tunnels are built to provide services
B. A layer that provides connectivity throughout the fabric
C. A term for everything in the SDN network
D. The controller's GUI
Answer: B - the book's review question 2. Option A is the overlay, and option C is the fabric.
Q2 Why should the underlay use only Layer 3 interfaces?
Answer: So STP does not run and block uplinks, and ECMP can balance traffic - STP would waste the fast redundant links.
Q3 Which OSPF network type removes the need for a DR on underlay links?
Answer: Point-to-point - ip ospf network point-to-point.
Q4 What does VXLAN do?
Answer: Tunnels Layer 2 traffic over a Layer 3 network - it lets VLANs span routed networks.
Q5 What must match for an OSPF adjacency to form, and what can you use if it does not?
Answer: The MTU, and ip ospf mtu-ignore - a mismatch stops OSPF neighbours from working properly.
Q1 What was DNA Center renamed?
A. Cisco Catalyst Center
B. Cisco Prime Center
C. Cisco Meraki Center
D. Cisco ACI Center
Answer: A - Cisco's data sheet says Catalyst Center is formerly DNA Center.
Q2 Which DNA Center feature is the "time machine"?
Answer: A - ssurance - it stores historical network data to look back at past issues.
Q3 Which feature configures new switches automatically using Plug and Play?
A. Path Trace
B. LAN Automation
C. EasyQoS
D. Command Runner
Answer: B - LAN Automation uses PnP with a DHCP server on the upstream device.
Q4 Which feature shows ACLs that would block a path?
Answer: Path Trace - traceroute cannot show that.
Q5 Can Command Runner push configuration?
Answer: No, only show commands - use Templates for configuration.
Q6 Name the three EasyQoS application categories.
Answer: B - usiness Relevant, Business Irrelevant, Default - applications can be moved between them.
Q7 How do scripts talk to DNA Center?
Answer: Through its REST API - Code Preview can generate snippets.
Q1 What do users and scripts use to interact with an SDN controller?
A. The southbound interface
B. The northbound interface
C. The data plane
D. The underlay
Answer: B - the NBI, usually a GUI or REST API.
Q2 Which interface does the controller use to configure network devices?
Answer: The southbound interface - examples: OpenFlow, NETCONF, OpFlex.
Q3 Which statement describes the underlay?
A. Virtual tunnels that provide services
B. The physical Layer 3 network that gives connectivity
C. A name for all devices in the solution
D. The controller's database
Answer: B - the overlay is the tunnels. The fabric is the term for everything.
Q4 Which statement describes the overlay?
Answer: A - virtual network tunnelled over the underlay, where services such as security and QoS are applied - VXLAN is the usual tunnel type.
Q5 What is a network fabric?
Answer: A - term for all the network devices that use the SDN solution (the underlay and overlay together) - the controller abstracts the details.
Q6 Which plane runs OSPF and ARP?
A. Management
B. Control
C. Data
D. Forwarding
Answer: B - the control plane runs protocols and builds forwarding information.
Q7 Which plane includes SSH, SNMP, HTTPS and the console port?
Answer: The management plane - it is how you reach and manage the device.
Q8 Which plane forwards traffic and drops packets denied by an ACL?
Answer: The data plane - it does not run protocols.
Q9 Which protocol does an NMS mainly use to poll devices?
A. SNMP
B. NETCONF
C. OpenFlow
D. OpFlex
Answer: A - an NMS polls with SNMP.
Q10 What is the difference between an SNMP poll and a trap?
Answer: A - poll is a request from the NMS. A trap is sent by the device on its own when an event happens - traps often carry more detail than syslog.
Q11 Which syslog severity number is "warnings", and which is "debugging"?
Answer: 4 and 7 - 0 is emergencies and 7 is debugging. A setting of N sends N and lower numbers.
Q12 Which command points a router at a syslog server?
A. logging host 10.1.1.1
B. logging trap 10.1.1.1
C. snmp-server host 10.1.1.1
D. syslog 10.1.1.1
Answer: A - logging trap sets the severity.
Q13 Name three things an NCM does.
Answer: B - ack up, compare, search and push configurations (any three) - templates are another.
Q14 Which table does CEF build from the routing table, and which table is built from ARP?
Answer: The FIB, and the adjacency table - both are in the data plane.
Q15 Which southbound protocol does OpenDaylight use, and which does Cisco ACI use?
Answer: OpenFlow and OpFlex - OpenFlow is imperative. OpFlex is declarative.
Q16 Which protocol uses XML over SSH, TCP port 830 by default?
A. NETCONF
B. OpenFlow
C. SNMP
D. onePK
Answer: A - RFC 6241 (Cisco IOS XE documentation). It models data with YANG.
Q17 In spine/leaf, which devices does a leaf connect to?
Answer: Every spine, and no other leaf - a leaf-to-leaf path is leaf, spine, leaf.
Q18 Why is STP a bad choice in an SDN underlay?
Answer: It blocks redundant links, wasting fast uplinks. Layer 3 links with ECMP use them all - use routed ports and OSPF instead.
Q19 Why use ip ospf network point-to-point on underlay links?
Answer: No DR/BDR election is needed - the neighbour state shows FULL with a dash instead of a DR role.
Q20 OSPF neighbours will not form after you changed system mtu on one switch. What are two fixes?
Answer: C - hange the MTU on the neighbouring switches too, or use ip ospf mtu-ignore - OSPF needs matching MTUs.
Q21 What does VXLAN do?
Answer: Tunnels Layer 2 traffic over a Layer 3 network - it lets VLANs span routed networks.
Q22 Which three technologies make up the SD-Access fabric?
Answer: LISP (control plane), VXLAN (data plane) and TrustSec (policy) - secondary Cisco sources. The book does not name them. CHECK
Q23 What is Cisco Catalyst Center's former name?
Answer: C - isco DNA Center - Cisco's data sheet says "formerly Cisco DNA Center".
Q24 Which DNA Center feature uses Plug and Play to configure new switches?
Answer: LAN Automation - a DHCP server on the upstream device gives the new device its address and the PnP server details.
Q25 Can Command Runner push configuration commands?
Answer: No, only show commands - use Templates for configuration.
Q26 Why is Path Trace better than traceroute?
Answer: It shows the true path including tunnels, Layer 2 switches and ACLs that would block traffic - traceroute shows only Layer 3 hops.
Q27 Name the three EasyQoS categories.
Answer: B - usiness Relevant, Business Irrelevant, Default - applications can be moved between them.
Q28 What is the main risk of pushing configuration from a controller?
Answer: A - mistake in a template is pushed to every device at once - review before applying.
Q29 Which v2.0 objective covers network management approaches such as controller-based and cloud-based?
Answer: 5.3 - official v2.0 outline. Controller, underlay and overlay details are not listed.
